analysis.title: Taking stock - Into 2027 after blue sweep
key_insights: Client views on the Democratic sweep diverge. One camp sees no derailment of US investment or dollar strength because the incoming Democratic bench is broad, limiting the risk of a sharp slowdown in capex and data center construction. The other camp sees US real rates at restrictive levels.
UBS sees EURUSD at 1.07 by Q2 '27. Some premium may leave the dollar, but the US remains the strongest major economy and further appreciation would not be surprising.
US rates and USD could fall quickly if AI capex disappoints relative to UBS's baseline of $1.75tn of hyperscaler capex in 2027.
Most clients met see 5% as a ceiling for the US 2y. Resilient activity, sticky inflation and strong equities could still drive front-end repricing.

After another strong November jobs report, investors expect the Fed to signal an accelerated reversal of its 75bp of 2025 'insurance' cuts, with 25bp hikes in December and January. This matches the UBS baseline.

Clients see a 50bp hike as requiring another hot November inflation report, but that data will not be available at the December FOMC. Some argued that core PCE trends could lead the Fed to signal in December that it has been too slow to hike, and that the dot plot still matters.

Some clients argued it is more attractive to fade ECB or BoE hikes than equivalent US moves. UBS thematically likes 5s30s SOFR curve steepeners, while some clients prefer a flatter 2s5s in the US. UBS expects the 2s10s ESTR curve to flatten further in Europe.

On AI, clients said the market may be underestimating Chinese competition and fragmentation of corporate demand. The open questions are who owns the infrastructure, controls the data and captures the monetization. Some clients said the equity wealth effect around AI capex may matter more for growth than the physical spending.

Some clients view the recent tech sell-off as partly technical, with de-grossing in AI and semiconductors offering a better entry point. Defensives are not cheap, so a further rotation away from AI was not seen as compelling.

UBS's 2027 outlook argues core yields are at better levels again, with some potential for global cyclical strength. Some clients want to see further fixed income performance before reallocating, given expected AI debt issuance.

ECB policy rates and energy prices will determine how far European spreads widen. The recent sell-off reflected French political risk, higher oil and an ECB reflation trade. A benign ECB path with stable or lower oil could let spreads normalise without a decisive improvement in French politics.

Clients pushed back on UBS's baseline of an ECB hike in March, with some expecting a final hike in December because of a weaker German labour market. The market prices 7bp for an ECB hike at the February '27 meeting. The consensus view is that an off-cycle hike between ECB outlook updates is very unlikely.

A renewed US-Iran confrontation is the principal tail risk. Higher energy prices could trigger a broader repricing of France and European spread products. Clients also questioned the resilience of French equities, which are up 2.5% year-to-date despite the spread widening.

UBS is cautious on French spreads in H1 2027 and more constructive afterwards. Political uncertainty, limited scope for consolidation before 2028 and higher debt-servicing costs argue for caution. Spreads of around 100-150bp could be justified while those risks persist.

Domestic savings are seen as a backstop for France, which has no large net external borrowing needs. Domestic institutions hold unusually low OAT exposure, so even a modest reallocation could tighten spreads meaningfully once politics stabilise.

UBS says France's debt-to-GDP is unlikely to stabilise before 2030. The 2028 budget may offer the first realistic chance of meaningful consolidation. Pension taxation and indexation could save money but will be politically hard to implement.

SNB Chair Schlegel said the SNB does not see inflationary pressures broadening despite an upside surprise, with rents a key source of pressure. Growth has been resilient. UBS's baseline is for a next SNB hike in March '27.

Politics around the next EU budget, including member-state contributions and future common borrowing, are shaping the premium in EU bonds. UBS reads this as a question about the future scale and permanence of the asset class, not the creditworthiness of existing debt.

UBS recommends staying defensive in covered bonds, favouring core markets and the 2-5Y sector for carry, relative value and defensiveness. German covereds are the preferred expression, with attractive relative value versus KfW and Länder. French politics, heavy EGB and SSA issuance and a busy primary calendar should keep spreads under pressure in H1.

sector_views.rationale: Defensive positioning preferred. Covereds were resilient during sovereign spread volatility, but French political uncertainty and heavy supply should keep spreads under pressure in H1. UBS favours core markets and the 2-5Y sector, with German covereds preferred.

tension_points.theme: US dollar and capex after blue sweep
tension_points.bull_case: The blue sweep is unlikely to derail US investment or the dollar. The broad Democratic bench limits the risk of a sharp slowdown in capex and data center construction, and the US remains the strongest major economy, with UBS seeing EURUSD at 1.07 by Q2 '27.
tension_points.bear_case: US real rates are at restrictive levels, so US rates and the USD could fall quickly if AI capex disappoints relative to UBS's $1.75tn 2027 hyperscaler baseline.
tension_points.what_invalidates: AI capex disappointment relative to the UBS baseline of $1.75tn of hyperscaler capex in 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: The recent technology sell-off looks partly technical, with de-grossing in AI and semiconductors potentially offering a better entry point. Defensives are not cheap.
tension_points.bear_case: The market may be underestimating Chinese competition and fragmentation of corporate demand, and AI debt issuance is expected to continue.
